company/recall: Batch norm rescued a unit stuck on the flat top of the sigmoid. Over a batch of four examples, its z was nine, three, seventeen and eleven. Batch norm slid them to center on zero, then squeezed them to a spread of one.
company/company: But each value was measured against the rest of its batch. Nine came out minus zero point two only because three, seventeen and eleven came along.
company/two: Put nine in a batch of two, beside three. Their mean is six, and each sits three away from it, so now nine becomes plus one.
company/always: Every batch of two ends the same way: the larger value becomes plus one and the smaller minus one, however far apart they are.
company/one: And in a batch of one, nine is its own mean, so it becomes zero. Whatever the input, the output is the same.
sideways/grid: Lay a batch out as before: one example per row, one feature per column. Our unit is column zero, and batch norm works down it, so every value leans on the rest of its column.
sideways/paper: In 2016, Jimmy Ba, Jamie Kiros and Geoffrey Hinton pointed out that this makes batch norm depend on the size of the batch. Their answer, in their words, was to transpose it: turn it sideways.
sideways/row: Layer normalization works along a row: one example's own features, and nothing else. Example zero's row is nine, one, fifteen and seven.
sideways/name: A row holds the value of every unit in a layer, for that one example. The mean and spread are taken across the whole layer, which gives layer norm its name.
sideways/alone: Now shrink the batch to one. Each column holds a single number, so batch norm turns every one into zero. The row still holds four, so layer norm still works.
sideways/same: Since nothing outside the row enters, the other examples can never change this one's result. Training and test do exactly the same arithmetic, with no running averages to keep.
one/x: Follow example zero along its row: nine, one, fifteen and seven, the values of the layer's four units for this one example.
one/mean: Together they make thirty two, so their mean, mu, is eight. Slide every value down by eight, and the row centers on zero.
one/var: The squared distances from the mean, one, forty nine, forty nine and one, average to twenty five: the variance.
one/sigma: Its square root, five, is the standard deviation, sigma. Squeeze every distance by it.
one/xhat: So nine, one above the mean, becomes one fifth: zero point two. The row now has mean zero and spread one, whatever else is in the batch.
one/gamma: Then come the learned scale and shift from batch norm, gamma and beta: one pair per feature, never per example.
one/scale: If feature zero's gamma is two and its beta is one, zero point two becomes two times zero point two, plus one: one point four.
one/count: Write d for the number of features. Each layer norm learns d scales and d shifts, two d in all, however big the batch: with five hundred twelve features, one thousand and twenty four.
